body.text: Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has aired the Japanese government’s deep concerns with the US sanctions against the ICC, stating that they are “incompatible with Japan’s position” (Rick Bajornas/UN Photo)
Australia should do more to back Japan and the ICC in the face of US sanctions
The US is sanctioning the ICC and its Japanese president – and Australia has offered little beyond private words.

Yet amid the festivities, Australia’s support for Japan has remained underwhelming in response to the US campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC). Japan has a longstanding connection to international criminal justice and the court, and was distressed after the US moved in August to sanction Judge Tomoko Akane, President of the ICC, a Japanese national, as well as senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye.

Australia’s relative silence has been just as noticeable in its relationship with Japan. In the two months since sanctions were imposed on the Japanese President of the ICC, none of the Australian Embassy in Japan’s social media accounts, whether Facebook, X, or LinkedIn, have referred to the sanctions and outlined Australia’s concerns. That includes a failure to reference the 9 October joint statement.

Quiet diplomacy appears to be Australia’s operating protocol in supporting its close partners who are impacted by the US sanctions. But discretion comes at a cost, with little visible solidarity being provided to Japan and defence of the court.

Australia’s response suggests that its “elevated relationship” with Japan has its limits when support risks confrontation with Washington. Concerns about angering the Trump administration, which is prone to unpredictable outbursts, appears to have led Canberra to favour discreet engagement.
Australia’s response to the US sanctions is a test of what its “indispensable partnership” with Japan means in practice.

After the latest US sanctions were imposed, Akane stated of the ICC that: “Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it.” Australia should heed Akane’s call. Quiet diplomacy on its own is not sufficient.
Australia should convert its private concerns into more credible public support with three steps.

Firstly, Australia should firmly denounce the US measures and express its solidarity with the Japanese government and Japanese nationals who have been targeted. Shared commitments to safeguarding the international order should lead to Australia choosing to act in their defence when like-minded partners are attacked.

Secondly, Australia should coordinate with Japan and other more vocal states to sustain political and diplomatic support for the ICC. Australia could play a stronger leadership role globally and regionally, including utilising international forums, to reinforce confidence in the court’s operations.

Thirdly, the Australian government should prevent US sanctions from being implemented in Australia and encourage regional partners to do the same. Banks, financial institutions and other companies should be advised against excessive overcompliance. This message should be delivered publicly.

The ICC is an independent and impartial body, mandated by the international community, to help bring the perpetrators of grave crimes to justice. Dismantling of the ICC will only serve to undermine the international rule of law, which is essential for promoting global order and security.

Australia should publicly defend the ICC, support its partners who are being targeted for upholding international justice, and demonstrate that its commitment to the international legal order can withstand US pressure.
